name: Temporal Color Grading Check
description: Validates color grading consistency across video timeline — AI video often has inconsistent color treatment between segments.
mechanism:
This method detects AI-generated or manipulated video by analyzing the temporal consistency of color grading — the overall color treatment that should remain stable within a single shot:

1. **Color Transfer Function Estimation**: The method models the color grading of each frame as a 3D color transfer function that maps scene illumination to display colors. This is estimated by computing the per-channel tone curves (R, G, B) from the histogram of each frame. For each channel, the method fits a parametric tone curve using a 4-parameter sigmoid model: f(x) = a + (b-a) / (1 + exp(-c(x-d))), which captures the typical S-curve shape of color grading with lift (shadows), gamma (midtones), and gain (highlights) adjustments. The 12 parameters (4 per channel) constitute the color grading signature of each frame. In a professionally graded or naturally captured shot, these parameters should remain constant (within-shot) or change only due to physical illumination changes.

2. **Intra-Shot Color Stability**: Within a continuous shot (between cuts), the color grading signature must remain temporally stable — the same scene viewed by the same camera under the same lighting should produce consistent colors. The method detects shot boundaries using histogram-difference and edge-change metrics, then measures the variation of the 12 tone curve parameters within each shot. For authentic video, the coefficient of variation of each parameter is < 0.03 within a shot. AI-generated video often shows per-frame color grading variations — subtle shifts in white balance, saturation, or contrast from frame to frame — because each frame may be processed through different generator states. The method flags shots where the intra-shot color parameter variance exceeds 3σ above the authentic threshold.

3. **Color Harmony Validation**: Professional color grading creates a coherent color palette — typically dominated by complementary pairs (teal-orange, blue-yellow) or analogous colors. The method analyzes the color distribution in CIE L*C*h° space and validates: (a) hue concentration — real graded footage shows 2–3 dominant hue clusters, while AI-generated video may show more scattered hue distributions, (b) saturation consistency — saturation levels should be consistent across regions with similar content (skin saturation 15–35 in L*C*h°), (c) shadow-highlight color split — in color-graded footage, shadows and highlights often have different hue biases (warm highlights, cool shadows) that should be temporally consistent. AI-generated video sometimes produces per-frame color palette shifts that violate the intended grading style.

4. **Cross-Object Color Consistency**: Within the same frame and across frames, objects of known color should maintain consistent chromaticity: (a) skin tones across different people should fall on the skin line (a narrow band in YCbCr space where Cb ≈ 100–120, Cr ≈ 135–160), (b) the same object appearing in multiple frames should have consistent color (tracked using appearance-based re-identification), (c) white and gray reference objects should indicate the same white balance. The method tracks these color anchors across time and flags temporal inconsistencies. AI-generated video may show the same person's skin tone shifting between warm and cool tints across frames, or background object colors drifting without corresponding illumination changes.
parameters:
Tone curve model: 4-parameter sigmoid per channel
Parameters per frame: 12 (4 × 3 channels)
Intra-shot CV threshold: < 0.03
Shot boundary detection: histogram difference + edge change
Skin tone range: Cb 100–120, Cr 135–160 (YCbCr)
Hue analysis: CIE L*C*h° space
Skin saturation range: C* 15–35
Dominant hue clusters: 2–3 expected
Color tracking: appearance-based re-ID
Analysis window: full shot duration
accuracy: 78–87% accuracy detecting AI-generated video via color grading analysis. Intra-shot stability achieves AUC of 0.85. Cross-object color consistency provides F1-score of 0.82. Performance highest for videos with consistent lighting and multiple trackable objects. Performance decreases for content with intentional color effects or rapid illumination changes.
source: Hsu, Y. F. & Chang, S. F. (2006). Detecting Image Splicing Using Geometry Invariants and Camera Characteristics. IEEE ICME, 549–552.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated video through per-frame color inconsistency. Forensic analysis of composite video where segments have different color grading. Validating temporal color coherence in deepfake detection. Identifying unauthorized color manipulation in broadcast content.
strengths:
• Color grading must be consistent within a shot — strong temporal constraint
• Tone curve parametrization captures the full color treatment
• Skin tone analysis provides a physiologically grounded color anchor
• Works for general video content without specific scene requirements
• Complementary to texture and motion-based forensic methods
limitations:
• Scenes with rapidly changing illumination (e.g., concert lighting) reduce reliability
• Heavily stylized content (music videos, art films) may have intentionally inconsistent color
• High dynamic range (HDR) content requires modified tone curve models
• Low-quality video with banding artifacts complicates tone curve estimation
• Some AI generators with temporal attention may maintain color consistency
